name: The Second Fundamental Theorem of Welfare Economics
statement: With convex preferences and production sets, every Pareto-efficient allocation can be achieved as a competitive equilibrium via lump-sum redistribution of endowments.
statementAccent: every Pareto-efficient allocation can be achieved as a competitive equilibrium
meaning: The theorem says efficiency and equity can, in principle, be separated: any Pareto-efficient outcome a society might prefer — not just the one markets happen to produce from existing endowments — can itself be supported by a competitive equilibrium, provided initial endowments or wealth are first redistributed via lump-sum transfers. Markets then only handle allocation, while distribution is handled by a one-time transfer.
mechanism: Because preferences and production sets are convex, a Pareto-efficient allocation can be supported by a hyperplane of prices separating each agent’s "at-least-as-good" set from the aggregate feasible set; those supporting prices, combined with lump-sum transfers giving each agent exactly the wealth to afford their assigned bundle, turn the target allocation into a genuine competitive equilibrium.

examples.text: The theorem is used to argue that a society wanting a more equal outcome need not abandon competitive markets — it can redistribute initial wealth via lump-sum taxes and transfers and then let market prices reach that more equal, still-efficient allocation.
Oskar Lange’s 1942 work established the now-standard pairing of the first and second theorems, and Arrow and Debreu gave rigorous convexity-based proofs of the second theorem around 1951.

The literature notes the theorem is of limited direct practical value because the required lump-sum transfers — redistribution that does not itself distort prices or incentives — are generally infeasible for real governments to implement.

whyItMatters: It underlies the standard economic case for addressing inequality through redistribution of endowments or wealth rather than price controls or output restrictions, since the latter sacrifice efficiency while idealised lump-sum transfers do not.
limits: It depends on convexity of preferences and production, on genuinely non-distortionary lump-sum transfers, and on complete information about individuals’ circumstances — none of which typically hold — which is why it is regarded as a much weaker policy guide than the first theorem.
misreadings: It is sometimes misread as a workable prescription ("just redistribute and let markets do the rest"), when real-world transfers are never truly lump-sum and always carry distortionary or informational cost.
origin: Traditionally paired with the first theorem by Oskar Lange in 1942; given rigorous convex-economy proofs by Kenneth Arrow and Gérard Debreu around 1951.

sources.text: Fundamental theorems of welfare economics, Wikipedia. — the second theorem’s convexity requirement, the need for lump-sum redistribution, and Lange’s 1942 pairing.
"Gérard Debreu," Encyclopaedia Britannica. — his rigorous reformulation of general-equilibrium theory including the convexity assumptions.
